Get a good night’s sleep.
Everyone knows that getting enough sleep is important, but how much do you know about the benefits of getting a good night’s sleep?
The National Sleep Foundation estimates that 80 percent of people with type 2 diabetes have at least one symptom they can manage and control — they usually get less than five hours of sleep per night.
You may also feel tired or sleepy after exercising too little or too many hours of exercise.
One thing you can do to help you fall asleep and stay healthy in the summer months is to avoid exercising too fast.
But the good news is that it’s not always easy to get a good night's sleep.
For example, many people who go into bed early after exercise will experience symptoms such as fatigue, lack of energy and feelings of restlessness.
Some studies suggest that more than half of people who are diagnosed with type 2 diabetes lose their sleep through the night.
And if you don’t get enough sleep, you can feel dizzy, sleepy and sluggish.
The truth is that there is no better way to fall asleep and stay asleep than by staying up late.

Kowalski's research team has an opportunity to work with other researchers in the field to better understand how coral reefs and their ability to support coral growth can be affected by factors like climate change.
Prof. Dr. Maria Kowalski is a specialist in the Coral Reef Research Centre at University of Liverpool who works alongside her colleagues on understanding coral reef structure and function. She also brings together experts from around the world working together to better understand the biological processes that help coral reefs thrive and to develop innovative strategies to protect them.
The first step is identifying the areas where corals have adapted to grow and are now under threat from climate change. This includes coral reefs that are particularly vulnerable to climate change. "We hope our research will help us understand how corals adapt to increasing temperatures," she said.
